doc.title: Peter Ecklund interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Growing up in the 1950s: classical and Broadway, not rock and roll
summary: Born in 1945, he heard mostly classical and Broadway music at home; rock was seen as delinquent music, and his parents supported his music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: A typical week — where do you live?
Okay. And you were born when?
Okay. So how come when you were oh twelve years old, in 1957, how come you didn’t get into Rock & roll? Or did you?

Well I didn’t hear any. I mean my parents had classical music and they had Broadway music and that was about it. And Rock & roll, I mean it was very strong at that time, but it kind of didn’t have the respectability among people who thought they were intellectuals that it had just a few years later, like when I went to college. It was kind of a hoodlums and juvenile delinquents’ music.

Right. It’s funny. It’s like it occupied the same role that rap music occupies now. But I mean The Beatles came out I guess just before I entered college. And that really changed everything, that meant that Rock took over popular music. But I really I mean I was familiar with it but it wasn’t a big part of my life. I just heard classical music and Broadway shows, Broadway music.
Were your parents supportive of your music endeavors?

Yeah. I mean I’m not so sure they were so happy when I became a musician, that was many years later, but they certainly supported my musical endeavors. I mean I was really doing nothing but classical music then, but I was interested in jazz, and listened to it a fair amount.
